answer: Amber — a form of social capital in this study — attained its highest value in the **4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE)**, peaking in the time interval **3300–3000 BCE**, where its Z-value reached its global maximum of **Zamber = 1.54** (calibrated **5250–4950 calBP**; **3300–3000 BCE** / **CE −3300 to −3000**). The high-value phase is sustained throughout the 4th millennium BCE: the interpolated amber Z-series stands at ≈1.46 across 4000–3400 BCE and rises to the 1.54 maximum plateau over 3300–3000 BCE, before falling to 0.37 by 2900 BCE. The maximum plateau itself (301 years at Zamber = 1.54) spans 3300–3000 BCE; although its final year (3000 BCE) is technically the last year of the 3rd millennium BCE, 300 of the 301 peak years fall inside the 4th millennium BCE, and the 4th millennium has by far the highest sustained amber value (within-millennium mean Z ≈ 1.49, versus ≈0.18–(−0.73) in all other millennia). Thus, the 4th millennium BCE hosts amber's peak, centered on the 3300–3000 BCE interval.
